chapters.title: I — Laying Plans
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: War is a matter of vital importance to the state.
It is a matter of life and death, the road to survival or destruction. It demands serious study — you cannot afford to ignore it.
War is governed by five fundamental factors. You must weigh all of them when assessing your strategic position.
These are: (1) Moral Authority; (2) Heaven; (3) Earth; (4) Leadership; (5) Method and Discipline.
Moral Authority means your people are fully aligned with their leader. They will follow him into danger without hesitation, willing to live or die for the cause.
Heaven refers to timing — night and day, cold and heat, the rhythm of the seasons.
Earth refers to terrain — distances near and far, danger and safety, open ground and chokepoints, the odds of survival.
Leadership encompasses wisdom, integrity, compassion, courage, and discipline.
Method and Discipline cover the organization of your forces, the chain of command, supply logistics, and the management of resources.
Every leader must master these five factors. Those who understand them will prevail. Those who do not will fail.
Therefore, when planning your strategy, use these factors as your framework for comparison. Ask yourself:
Which leader commands greater moral authority from their people?
Which commander is more capable? Who holds the advantage of timing and terrain?
Which side enforces discipline more rigorously? Which force is stronger?
Which side has better-trained officers and soldiers?
Which side is more consistent in its rewards and punishments?
Through these seven comparisons, I can predict victory or defeat.
The leader who follows my counsel and acts on it will win — keep that leader in command. The leader who ignores my counsel will lose — remove that leader immediately.
While applying my strategic principles, also seize any situational advantages that arise beyond the standard playbook.
Adapt your plans as circumstances shift.
All warfare is based on deception.
When you are able to strike, appear unable. When you are active, appear passive. When you are close, make the enemy think you are far away. When far away, make them think you are near.
Dangle bait to lure the enemy. Feign chaos, then crush them.
If the enemy is well fortified, prepare for a long engagement. If they are stronger, avoid direct confrontation.
If the enemy commander has a short temper, provoke him. If he is arrogant, appear weak to feed his overconfidence.
If the enemy is resting, give them no peace.
If their forces are unified, split them apart.
Strike where they are not prepared. Appear where they do not expect you.
These strategic principles that lead to victory must never be revealed in advance.
The leader who wins a battle has done extensive planning before the fight begins.

The leader who loses has done little planning beforehand. Thorough planning leads to victory; poor planning leads to defeat — and no planning at all? That is guaranteed failure. By this standard alone, I can see who will win and who will lose.

chapters.title: II — Waging War
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: When launching a major military operation — a thousand fast chariots, a thousand heavy chariots, a hundred thousand armored soldiers, with supplies for a long campaign — the total cost at home and in the field, including diplomatic expenses, equipment maintenance, and vehicle and armor repairs, will reach a thousand ounces of silver per day. That is the price of fielding an army of 100,000.
When you commit to actual combat, if victory takes too long, your troops will grow weary and their morale will collapse. Besiege a city, and you will drain your strength.
A prolonged campaign will exhaust the nation's resources.

When your weapons are blunted, your morale shattered, your strength spent, and your treasury empty, rival powers will exploit your weakness. At that point, no amount of wisdom can save you from the consequences.
Speed in war may sometimes be clumsy, but no one has ever seen brilliance come from dragging things out.
No nation has ever benefited from a prolonged war.
Only someone who truly understands the costs of war can understand how to wage it effectively.
A skilled commander does not conscript troops twice or resupply more than once.
Bring your equipment from home, but take your food from the enemy. That way, your army will never go hungry.
When a state funds a distant army from its own treasury, the people at home are impoverished. Maintaining supply lines over long distances bleeds a nation dry.
Meanwhile, the presence of an army drives up local prices, and rising prices drain the people's wealth.
When their wealth is drained, the people are crushed by heavier taxes.

This loss of wealth and exhaustion of strength strips households bare. The people lose up to three-tenths of their income, while the government's expenses for damaged equipment, worn-out horses, weapons, armor, and transport consume four-tenths of state revenue.

A wise commander therefore makes it a priority to feed his army from enemy territory. One cartload of the enemy's provisions is worth twenty of your own, and one measure of their fodder equals twenty of yours.
To motivate soldiers to kill the enemy, you need to stoke their fighting spirit. To motivate them to seize the enemy's resources, you need to reward them.

In a chariot engagement, when ten or more enemy chariots are captured, reward the soldier who seized the first one. Replace the enemy's banners with your own, mix captured chariots into your fleet, and treat captured soldiers well.
This is what it means to use the conquered enemy to grow your own strength.
In war, pursue decisive victory — not drawn-out campaigns.
The commander of an army holds the fate of the people in his hands. He determines whether the nation lives in peace or faces ruin.

chapters.title: III — Attack by Stratagem
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: The supreme art of war is to take the enemy's territory intact, not to destroy it. It is better to capture an army whole than to annihilate it — the same applies to a regiment, a detachment, or a company.
Winning every battle through fighting is not the highest achievement. The highest achievement is breaking the enemy's resistance without fighting at all.

The best form of strategy is to disrupt the enemy's plans. The next best is to prevent their forces from uniting. After that, engage their army in the field. The worst option is to besiege fortified cities.
The rule: never besiege a city if you can possibly avoid it.
Building siege equipment and preparing earthworks will take months of preparation — three months for the equipment alone, and another three for the assault ramps.
A commander who cannot control his frustration will throw his soldiers at the walls like ants. A third of his men will die, and the city will remain untaken. That is the catastrophe of a siege.
The skillful leader therefore defeats the enemy without fighting, captures cities without besieging them, and overthrows nations without prolonged campaigns.
With his forces intact, he contests for supremacy. Without losing a single soldier, his victory is complete.
This is the method of strategic attack.
The rule of engagement: if you outnumber the enemy ten to one, surround them. Five to one, attack. Two to one, divide your force.
If evenly matched, you can engage. If slightly outnumbered, avoid contact. If completely outmatched, retreat.
A small force may fight stubbornly, but it will eventually be overwhelmed by a larger one.
The commander is the backbone of the state. When the commander is strong in every respect, the state is strong. When the commander is flawed, the state is vulnerable.
A ruler can bring disaster upon his own army in three ways:
First, by ordering the army to advance or retreat without understanding the tactical reality on the ground. This hobbles the army.
Second, by trying to manage the military the same way he administers civilian affairs, without understanding how armies operate. This creates confusion in the ranks.
Third, by assigning officers without regard for their abilities, ignoring the principle of matching people to roles. This destroys the soldiers' confidence.
When an army is confused and demoralized, rivals will exploit the opening. This is what it means to invite chaos into your own ranks and throw victory away.
There are five keys to victory: The leader who knows when to fight and when to hold back will win.
The leader who knows how to deploy both large and small forces will win.
The leader whose entire organization shares a unified purpose will win.
The leader who is prepared and catches the enemy unprepared will win.
The leader who has military competence and is not micromanaged from above will win.
Victory comes from understanding these five principles.
Hence the saying: Know your enemy and know yourself, and you will win a hundred battles. Know yourself but not the enemy, and for every victory you will suffer a defeat.
Know neither your enemy nor yourself, and you will lose every battle.

chapters.title: IV — Tactical Dispositions
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: The great warriors of the past first made themselves invincible, then waited for the enemy to become vulnerable.
Making yourself unbeatable is within your control. Whether the enemy gives you an opening is up to them.
A skilled fighter can make himself invincible, but he cannot guarantee he will defeat the enemy.
Hence the saying: You can know how to win without being able to make it happen.
Defending against defeat requires defensive tactics. Defeating the enemy requires going on offense.
Choosing defense signals insufficient strength. Choosing attack signals overwhelming strength.
The master of defense hides as if beneath the deepest layers of earth. The master of attack strikes as if from the highest reaches of the sky.
In this way, you protect yourself completely on one hand — and achieve total victory on the other.
Seeing victory only when it is obvious to everyone is not the mark of excellence.
Winning a battle that the whole world applauds is not the mark of excellence either.
As the saying goes: what truly matters is invisible to the casual observer.
Lifting a feather is no test of strength. Seeing the sun and moon requires no special vision. Hearing thunder demands no sharp ears.
What the ancients called a brilliant fighter was someone who won with apparent ease.
The brilliant fighter's victories earn him no reputation for genius and no credit for bravery.
He wins by making zero mistakes.
Making zero mistakes is what guarantees victory — because it means defeating an enemy who is already beaten.
The skilled fighter puts himself in a position where defeat is impossible, and never misses the moment to strike the enemy.
A victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory is already assured. A defeated one fights first and then hopes for the best.
The masterful leader cultivates moral authority and enforces method and discipline. With these, he controls the outcome.
Military method consists of five steps: Measurement, Assessment, Calculation, Comparison, and Victory.
Measurement comes from terrain. Assessment comes from measurement. Calculation comes from assessment. Comparison comes from calculation. Victory comes from comparison.
A victorious army versus a beaten one is like placing a full pound on a scale against a single grain.
The force of a victorious army unleashed is like a torrent of water crashing into a chasm a thousand feet deep. That is what tactical positioning makes possible.

chapters.title: V — Energy
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: Managing a large force uses the same principles as managing a small one. It is simply a matter of organization and structure.
Commanding a large army in battle works the same as commanding a small one. It is simply a matter of clear communication — signals and signs.
Ensuring your entire force can absorb the enemy's attack without breaking — that is achieved through the interplay of direct and indirect methods.
Making your strike as devastating as a millstone dropped on an egg — that is achieved through understanding where the enemy is strong and where he is weak.
In any battle, the direct approach is used to engage the enemy, but indirect methods are what deliver victory.

Indirect tactics, skillfully applied, are as infinite as heaven and earth, as inexhaustible as rivers and streams. Like the sun and moon, they set only to rise again. Like the seasons, they end only to return.
There are only five musical notes, yet their combinations produce more melodies than can ever be heard.
There are only five primary colors, yet their combinations produce more shades than the eye can distinguish.
There are only five basic tastes — sour, pungent, salty, sweet, and bitter — yet their combinations yield more flavors than can ever be sampled.
In battle, there are only two methods — direct and indirect — yet their combination generates an infinite variety of tactics.
Direct and indirect flow into each other in an endless cycle. It is like moving in a circle — there is no end. Who could exhaust the possibilities?
The momentum of troops in action is like a torrent powerful enough to roll boulders downstream.
The quality of timing is like a falcon's strike — precise, swift, and devastating.
The great fighter is ferocious in momentum and razor-sharp in timing.
Energy is like drawing a crossbow. Timing is like releasing the bolt.
In the chaos of battle, there may appear to be disorder, but there is no real disorder. In the confusion of the melee, your formation may seem shapeless, yet it remains unbreakable.
Apparent disorder requires perfect discipline underneath. Apparent fear requires real courage underneath. Apparent weakness requires actual strength underneath.

Hiding order behind a mask of disorder is a matter of organization. Hiding courage behind a show of timidity requires deep reserves of energy. Masking strength with apparent weakness is a matter of tactical positioning.
The commander who keeps the enemy reacting maintains deceptive appearances that the enemy cannot resist acting on.
He offers sacrificial bait that the enemy cannot help but grab.
He dangles rewards to keep the enemy moving, then ambushes them with his best troops.
The brilliant commander relies on the power of combined momentum, not on the heroics of individuals.
He selects the right people and unleashes their collective force.

When you harness combined momentum, your soldiers become like boulders on a slope. A boulder sits still on flat ground but rolls when placed on an incline. Square stones stop; round stones keep rolling.
The energy of well-led soldiers is like a round boulder rolling down a mountain thousands of feet high. That is the nature of strategic energy.

chapters.title: VI — Weak Points and Strong
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: Whoever arrives at the battlefield first and waits for the enemy will be fresh. Whoever arrives second and rushes into battle will be exhausted.
The skilled fighter imposes his will on the enemy and never allows the enemy to impose its will on him.
By offering advantages, you can draw the enemy to where you want them. By threatening damage, you can keep them away.
If the enemy is resting, harass them. If well supplied, cut off their food. If settled in camp, force them to move.
Appear at positions the enemy must rush to defend. March swiftly to places they do not expect.
An army can march great distances without strain if it moves through territory the enemy has left undefended.
You will always succeed in attack if you target positions that are undefended.
You will always hold your defense if you occupy positions that cannot be attacked.
The attacker whose opponent does not know what to defend is masterful. The defender whose opponent does not know what to attack is masterful.
The supreme art of subtlety and secrecy! Through it we become invisible, inaudible — and we hold the enemy's fate in our hands.
You can advance irresistibly if you strike at the enemy's weak points. You can withdraw safely if your speed exceeds the enemy's.
If you want to fight, you can force the enemy to engage even behind high walls and deep ditches. Just attack something they are compelled to defend.
If you do not want to fight, you can prevent engagement even with the barest of defenses. Just present the enemy with something unexpected and confusing.
By uncovering the enemy's dispositions while concealing your own, you can concentrate your forces while the enemy must scatter theirs.
When you are concentrated and the enemy is scattered, you pit your whole against their parts. You will be many against their few.
If you can attack a smaller force with a larger one, your opponent is in serious trouble.
Never reveal where you intend to fight. This forces the enemy to defend everywhere at once, spreading their forces thin. At any given point of contact, you will outnumber them.

Strengthen the front, and the rear weakens. Strengthen the rear, and the front weakens. Reinforce the left, the right suffers. Reinforce the right, the left suffers. Try to reinforce everything, and everything is weak.
Weakness comes from having to defend everywhere. Strength comes from forcing your enemy to defend everywhere.
If you know where and when the battle will happen, you can concentrate your forces from any distance.

If you know neither the place nor the time, your left flank cannot support the right, the right cannot support the left, the front cannot support the rear, nor the rear the front. This is even more true when your forces are separated by great distances.
Even if the enemy outnumbers us, that advantage counts for nothing if we control the terms of engagement. Victory can be engineered.
Even against superior numbers, you can prevent the enemy from fighting on their terms. Probe their plans and assess the likelihood of success.
Provoke the enemy and observe their patterns of action and inaction.
Force them to reveal themselves, and you will discover their vulnerabilities.
Compare the opposing force with your own to identify where you have excess strength and where you are deficient.

The highest achievement in tactical positioning is to make your dispositions invisible. When your positions are hidden, even the best spies cannot find them and the cleverest strategists cannot plan against them.
Turning the enemy's own tactics into their defeat — that is what most people cannot grasp.
Everyone can see the tactics by which I win, but no one can see the underlying strategy from which victory emerges.
Never repeat the same winning tactic. Let your methods be shaped by the infinite variety of circumstances.
Military strategy is like water. Water naturally flows downhill, away from high ground.
In war, the principle is the same: avoid the enemy's strengths and strike at their weaknesses.
Water shapes its course according to the terrain. The soldier shapes his victory according to the enemy he faces.
Just as water has no fixed shape, warfare has no fixed formula.
The commander who can adapt his tactics to match the enemy and still achieve victory deserves to be called a genius.
The five elements are never equally dominant. The four seasons cycle endlessly.
Days grow long and short. The moon waxes and wanes. Everything changes — so must your strategy.

chapters.title: VII — Maneuvering
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: In war, the commander receives orders from the sovereign.
After assembling and organizing the army, he must unify its elements before establishing his position.
After that comes tactical maneuvering — the most difficult part of warfare.
The challenge of maneuvering lies in turning indirect routes into direct ones, and turning setbacks into advantages.
To take a long, roundabout path while luring the enemy off course, then arrive at the objective before them — that demonstrates mastery of indirect approach.
Maneuvering with a disciplined army is advantageous. Maneuvering with an undisciplined mob is disastrous.
If you march your entire equipped army to seize an advantage, you will likely arrive too late. But if you send a fast detachment, it goes without its supplies.
If you force your soldiers to march day and night without rest, covering double the normal distance to seize an advantage a hundred miles away, all three of your division commanders may be captured.
The strongest soldiers will arrive first, the exhausted will straggle behind, and only a tenth of your force will reach the destination.
Force-march fifty miles for an advantage, and you will lose your lead commander. Only half your force will arrive.
Force-march thirty miles, and two-thirds will make it.
An army without its supply train is lost. Without provisions, it is lost. Without bases of supply, it is lost.
You cannot form alliances without knowing your neighbors' intentions.
You cannot lead an army through unfamiliar country without knowing the terrain — its mountains, forests, cliffs, and swamps.
You cannot exploit natural advantages without using local guides.
In war, practice deception and you will succeed.
Move only when there is a real advantage to be gained.
Whether to concentrate or divide your forces must be decided by the situation.
Move as fast as the wind. Hold formation like a forest.
In attack, be as destructive as fire. In defense, be as immovable as a mountain.
Keep your plans as dark and impenetrable as night. When you strike, hit like a thunderbolt.
When you plunder territory, distribute the spoils among your troops. When you capture new land, divide the benefits among your soldiers.
Think carefully before you act.
The commander who masters the art of indirect approach will prevail. That is the essence of maneuvering.

The Book of Army Management says: On the battlefield, the spoken word does not carry far enough — hence the use of drums and gongs. Normal visual signals are not clear enough — hence the use of banners and flags.
Drums, gongs, banners, and flags serve a single purpose: to focus the attention of the entire army on one point.
When the army acts as one body, the brave cannot advance alone, and the cowardly cannot retreat alone.
That is the art of managing large forces.
In night fighting, use signal fires and drums. In daytime fighting, use flags and banners. These tools control what your army sees and hears.
An entire army can have its spirit broken. A commander can have his composure shattered.
A soldier's energy peaks in the morning, fades by midday, and collapses by evening.
A skilled commander avoids the enemy when their spirit is high and attacks when they are sluggish and ready to quit. This is the art of managing morale.
Stay disciplined and calm while waiting for the enemy to become disordered and chaotic. This is the art of maintaining composure.
Stay close to the objective while the enemy is far from it. Rest while the enemy is exhausting itself. Be well-fed while the enemy goes hungry. This is the art of conserving strength.
Do not engage an enemy whose formations are in perfect order. Do not attack an army that is calm and confident. This is the art of reading circumstances.
Never advance uphill against the enemy. Never oppose an enemy charging downhill.
Do not pursue an enemy that fakes retreat. Do not attack soldiers whose fighting spirit is at its peak.
Do not take bait the enemy offers.
Do not block an army heading home.
When you surround the enemy, leave them an escape route. Do not press a cornered enemy too hard.
That is the art of warfare.

chapters.title: VIII — Variation in Tactics
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: In war, the commander receives orders from the sovereign, assembles the army, and concentrates forces.
Do not camp in difficult terrain. In areas where roads intersect, build alliances. Do not linger in exposed, isolated positions.
In confined situations, use ingenuity. In desperate situations, fight.
Some roads should not be taken. Some armies should not be attacked. Some cities should not be besieged. Some positions should not be contested. Some orders from above should not be obeyed.
The commander who truly understands the advantages of tactical flexibility knows how to deploy troops effectively.
The commander who does not understand this may know the terrain perfectly, yet be unable to turn that knowledge into results.
The student of war who cannot adapt his plans — even if he knows the Five Advantages — will fail to get the most from his forces.
The wise leader's plans always weigh both advantage and disadvantage together.
By factoring in potential downsides even when the outlook is favorable, you can accomplish your core objectives.
By looking for opportunities even in the middle of crisis, you can escape disaster.
Subdue rival leaders by inflicting damage on them. Create problems for them. Keep them constantly occupied. Dangle attractive bait and make them chase it.

The art of war teaches us not to rely on the hope that the enemy will not come, but on our own readiness. Not on the chance that they will not attack, but on the fact that we have made ourselves unassailable.

Five dangerous flaws can destroy a commander: (1) Recklessness, which leads to destruction. (2) Cowardice, which leads to capture. (3) A hot temper, which can be exploited through provocation. (4) Excessive pride, which makes him vulnerable to insult.
(5) Over-attachment to his troops, which opens him to anxiety and manipulation.
These five flaws are fatal in a commander and ruinous in war.
When an army is destroyed and its leader killed, the cause will always trace back to one of these five flaws. Study them carefully.

chapters.title: IX — The Army on the March
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: When positioning your army and reading the enemy's movements, cross mountains quickly and stay near valleys.
Camp on high ground, facing the sun.
Do not fight uphill. That is the rule for mountain warfare.
After crossing a river, move well away from it.
When the enemy crosses a river toward you, do not meet them in midstream. Let half their army cross, then attack.
If you want a fight, do not position yourself right next to a river the enemy must cross.
Anchor your position upstream and facing the sun.
Do not advance upstream against the enemy. That is the rule for river warfare.
When crossing marshlands, your only goal is to get through them quickly, without delay.
If forced to fight in a marsh, position yourself near water and grass with trees at your back. That is the rule for marsh warfare.
On flat, dry ground, take an accessible position with high ground to your right and rear — danger in front, safety behind. That is the rule for open terrain.
These are the four essential types of terrain knowledge.
This knowledge enabled the Yellow Emperor to defeat four rival sovereigns.
All armies prefer high ground to low, and sunlight to shadow.
If you take care of your soldiers and camp on solid ground, the army will be free from disease — and that means victory.
When you reach a hill or riverbank, occupy the sunny side with the slope to your right and rear. This benefits your soldiers and gives you the advantage of terrain.
When heavy rains upstream cause a river to flood and foam, wait for it to subside before crossing.
Terrain with steep cliffs and rushing torrents, deep hollows,
confined spaces, dense thickets, bogs,
and crevasses — leave all such places immediately and never approach them.
Keep your own forces away from such terrain while maneuvering the enemy toward it. Face these obstacles while ensuring the enemy has them at their back.
If your camp is near hills, ponds with tall grass, basins filled with reeds, or dense undergrowth, search them thoroughly. These are perfect hiding places for ambushes and spies.
When the enemy is close but stays quiet, they are relying on a strong position.
When the enemy keeps their distance but tries to provoke a fight, they want you to advance.
When the enemy camps in an easily accessible position, they are baiting you.
Movement in the trees means the enemy is advancing.
Screens placed in thick grass mean the enemy wants to make you suspicious.
Birds suddenly taking flight signals an ambush.
Startled animals mean a surprise attack is coming.
Dust rising in a tall column signals chariots or vehicles. Dust spread low and wide signals infantry on the move.
Dust branching in different directions means parties are out gathering supplies. Scattered small dust clouds mean the army is making camp.
Humble words combined with increased preparations mean the enemy is about to attack.
Aggressive language and a show of force mean the enemy is about to retreat.
When light vehicles move to the flanks, the enemy is forming for battle.
Peace proposals without formal guarantees signal a trap.
When there is a flurry of activity
and soldiers fall into formation, the decisive moment has arrived.
When some troops advance and others pull back, it is a lure.
When soldiers lean on their weapons, they are starving.
When those sent for water drink before returning, the army is dying of thirst.
When the enemy sees a clear advantage but does nothing, the soldiers are too exhausted to act.
Birds gathering on a position means it is unoccupied. Noise in the night means the troops are anxious.
Disturbance in camp means the commander has lost authority. Shifting banners and flags mean mutiny is brewing. Angry officers mean the soldiers are worn out.

When an army feeds grain to its horses and slaughters its cattle for food, and when soldiers do not hang their cooking pots over fires — meaning they will not return to camp — they are preparing for a fight to the death.
Soldiers whispering in small groups signals discontent in the ranks.
Excessive rewards mean the enemy is running out of options. Excessive punishments signal desperation.
A commander who starts with bluster but then shrinks from the enemy's numbers shows profound incompetence.
When the enemy sends envoys with flattering words, they want a ceasefire.
When the enemy's troops march up aggressively but hold position without attacking or withdrawing, the situation demands extreme vigilance.
If our forces are roughly equal to the enemy's, that is sufficient — it simply means we cannot launch a frontal assault.
Focus on concentrating available strength, watching the enemy closely, and securing reinforcements.
A commander who underestimates the enemy and fails to plan will be captured.
If you punish soldiers before earning their loyalty, they will not obey — and disobedient soldiers are useless. But if soldiers are loyal and discipline is not enforced, they are equally useless.
Treat soldiers with respect, then hold them to iron discipline. This is the proven path to victory.
When training standards are consistently enforced, the army will be well disciplined. When they are not, discipline will be poor.
A commander who shows genuine confidence in his troops while always insisting on obedience will earn mutual loyalty.

chapters.title: X — Terrain
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: There are six types of terrain: (1) Accessible ground; (2) Entangling ground; (3) Stalemate ground; (4) Narrow passes; (5) Steep heights; (6) Positions far from the enemy.
Ground that both sides can freely cross is accessible.
On accessible ground, occupy the high, sunny positions first and secure your supply lines.
Then you can fight with advantage.
Ground you can leave but cannot easily return to is entangling.
On entangling ground, if the enemy is unprepared, strike and defeat them. But if they are ready and you fail to win, you cannot retreat — and disaster follows.
Ground where neither side benefits from moving first is stalemate ground.
On stalemate ground, even if the enemy offers tempting bait, do not advance. Instead, pull back and lure the enemy forward. When part of their force has committed, strike with advantage.
With narrow passes, if you get there first, garrison them heavily and wait for the enemy.
If the enemy occupies a narrow pass first, do not attack if it is fully garrisoned. Only attack if the garrison is weak.
With steep heights, if you arrive first, take the high, sunny ground and wait for the enemy.
If the enemy holds the heights first, do not follow. Retreat and try to draw them down.
If you are far from the enemy and both forces are equal, it is difficult to provoke battle, and fighting will be disadvantageous.
These are the six principles of terrain.
Any commander in a position of responsibility must study them carefully.
There are six types of army failure that come not from nature but from the commander's mistakes: (1) Flight; (2) Insubordination; (3) Collapse; (4) Ruin; (5) Disorganization; (6) Rout.
When a force is thrown against one ten times its size, the result is flight.
When soldiers are too aggressive and officers too weak, the result is insubordination.
When officers are too overbearing and soldiers too passive, the result is collapse.
When senior officers are resentful and insubordinate, engaging the enemy on their own initiative out of spite without their commander's authorization, the result is ruin.
When the commander is weak and lacks authority, when orders are unclear, when there are no defined roles, and when formations are sloppy and disorganized, the result is total disorganization.

When a commander cannot assess the enemy's strength and sends a small force against a large one, or a weak detachment against a powerful one, without placing his best soldiers at the front, the result is a rout.
These are the six paths to defeat. Any commander in a position of responsibility must study them carefully.
Terrain is the soldier's greatest ally. But the ability to assess the enemy, control the conditions for victory, and accurately calculate risks and distances — that is the mark of a great commander.
The commander who understands these things and applies them in battle will win. The one who does not understand and does not apply them will surely lose.
If analysis says you will win, then fight — even if the ruler says not to. If analysis says you will lose, then do not fight — even if the ruler orders it.
The commander who advances without seeking glory and retreats without fearing blame, whose only purpose is to protect the people and serve the state, is the most valuable asset a nation can have.
Treat your soldiers as your own children, and they will follow you into the deepest danger. Treat them as your beloved sons, and they will stand with you until death.
But if you are generous without enforcing authority, kind without demanding obedience, and unable to maintain order — then your soldiers are like spoiled children, useless for any real purpose.
If we know our troops can attack but do not know the enemy is vulnerable, we are only halfway to victory.
If we know the enemy is vulnerable but do not know our own troops are ready, we are only halfway to victory.
If we know the enemy is vulnerable and our troops are ready, but ignore the terrain, we are still only halfway to victory.
The experienced commander, once in motion, is never confused. Once committed, he is never at a loss.
Hence the saying: Know the enemy and know yourself, and your victory is certain. Know heaven and know earth, and your victory is complete.

chapters.title: XI — The Nine Situations
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: The art of war recognizes nine types of ground: (1) Dispersive ground; (2) Frontier ground; (3) Contested ground; (4) Open ground; (5) Crossroads ground; (6) Serious ground; (7) Difficult ground; (8) Enclosed ground; (9) Death ground.
When you fight in your own territory, that is dispersive ground.
When you have entered enemy territory but not deeply, that is frontier ground.
Ground that would give a major advantage to whichever side holds it is contested ground.
Ground that both sides can move across freely is open ground.
Ground at the junction of three territories — whoever holds it gains access to all of them — is crossroads ground.
When you have penetrated deep into enemy territory with fortified positions behind you, that is serious ground.
Mountain forests, rugged terrain, marshes, and swamps — any land that is hard to traverse — this is difficult ground.
Ground reached through narrow approaches, where retreat requires winding paths, and where a small enemy force could destroy a much larger one — this is enclosed ground.
Ground where survival depends on fighting without hesitation — this is death ground.
On dispersive ground, do not fight. On frontier ground, do not stop. On contested ground, do not attack head-on.
On open ground, do not try to block the enemy.
On crossroads ground, build alliances.
On serious ground, secure supplies.
On difficult ground, keep moving.
On enclosed ground, use ingenuity. On death ground, fight.

The great leaders of the past knew how to split the enemy's front from rear, prevent their divisions from supporting each other, stop their officers from rallying their troops, and keep quality units from rescuing weaker ones.
When the enemy was scattered, they prevented regrouping. When the enemy was assembled, they kept them in chaos.
They advanced when it served their advantage. Otherwise, they held still.
If asked how to face a large, well-organized enemy force about to attack, I would say: Seize something they value deeply. Then they will do whatever you want.
Speed is the essence of war. Exploit the enemy's unreadiness. Take unexpected routes. Strike unguarded positions.
The principles for an invading force: The deeper you penetrate into enemy territory, the stronger your troops' cohesion becomes, and the harder it is for defenders to stop you.
Forage in rich territory to keep your army fed.
Take care of your soldiers and do not overwork them. Conserve energy and build reserves.
Keep the army moving and make your plans impossible to predict.
Put your soldiers in positions where there is no escape, and they will choose death over flight. When they are willing to die, there is nothing they cannot accomplish.
Officers and soldiers alike will fight with everything they have.
Soldiers in desperate situations lose their fear. With nowhere to run, they stand firm. Deep in hostile territory, they become resolute. With no alternative, they fight ferociously.
Under these conditions, soldiers are automatically vigilant without being told, loyal without being asked, devoted without restrictions, and trustworthy without orders.
Ban superstition and eliminate irrational fears. Then, until death itself arrives, there is nothing to be afraid of.
If soldiers are not burdened with wealth, it is not because they dislike riches. If they do not expect long lives, it is not because they reject longevity.
On the day they are ordered into battle, your soldiers may weep — tears running down their cheeks as they sit or lie waiting.
But once committed to the fight, they will show the courage of legends.
The skillful tactician is like the shuai-jan — a snake found in the mountains.
Strike its head, and the tail attacks. Strike its tail, and the head attacks. Strike its middle, and both head and tail attack.

Can an army be made to act like this snake? Yes. Consider this: the people of Wu and Yue are enemies. Yet if they are in the same boat caught in a storm, they will help each other just as the left hand helps the right.
Relying on hobbled horses and buried wheels is not enough to ensure discipline.
The principle of army management is to set a single standard of courage that all must meet.
How to get the best from both strong and weak soldiers — that is a matter of exploiting terrain.
The skilled general leads his entire army as if he were taking a single person by the hand.
A general must be calm and ensure secrecy. He must be fair and maintain order.
He must be able to deceive his own officers and soldiers with false reports and appearances, keeping them in total ignorance of the real plan.
By constantly changing arrangements and altering plans, he keeps the enemy guessing.
By shifting camps and taking roundabout routes, he prevents the enemy from anticipating his moves.
At the decisive moment, the leader acts like someone who climbs a height and kicks away the ladder. He takes his army deep into enemy territory before revealing his intentions.
He burns his boats and smashes his cooking pots. Like a shepherd driving sheep, he moves his men here and there, and no one knows where they are going.
Assembling the army and leading it into danger — that is the general's job.
The tactics suited to each of the nine types of ground, the balance between offense and defense, and the fundamental laws of human nature — these must be thoroughly studied.
When invading enemy territory, the general principle is: deep penetration creates unity; shallow penetration creates fragmentation.
When you leave your own territory and take your army through neighboring lands, you are on critical ground.
When routes connect in all directions, you are on crossroads ground.
When you have penetrated deeply, you are on serious ground. When you have barely entered, you are on frontier ground.
When the enemy's strongholds are behind you and narrow passes ahead, you are on enclosed ground. When there is no way out, you are on death ground.
On dispersive ground, I would unite my army's purpose.
On frontier ground, I would keep all units closely connected.
On contested ground, I would rush my reserves forward.
On open ground, I would focus on solid defense. On crossroads ground, I would strengthen alliances.
On serious ground, I would ensure a steady flow of supplies.
On difficult ground, I would keep pressing forward along the road.
On enclosed ground, I would block all escape routes.
On death ground, I would make it clear to my soldiers that there is no possibility of survival except through fighting.
It is human nature to resist stubbornly when surrounded, to fight ferociously when cornered, and to follow orders instantly when in mortal danger.

You cannot ally with neighboring powers until you understand their intentions. You cannot lead an army through unfamiliar country without knowing the terrain. You cannot exploit natural advantages without local guides.
To be ignorant of any of these principles is unfit for a commander.
When a powerful leader attacks a strong state, his skill shows in preventing the enemy from concentrating. He intimidates his opponents, and their allies dare not join against him.
Therefore he does not seek alliances with everyone, nor does he build up the power of other states. He pursues his own strategy in secret, keeping his enemies in a state of fear.
In this way, he captures cities and overthrows kingdoms.
Distribute rewards without following the usual rules. Issue orders
without following established precedent. You can then command an entire army as if directing a single person.
Confront your soldiers with the mission itself — never reveal your plans in advance.
When the situation is favorable, let them see it. When the situation is grim, tell them nothing.
Place your army in mortal danger, and it will survive. Plunge it into desperate straits, and it will come through safely.
It is precisely when an army faces destruction that it is capable of winning.
Success in war comes from carefully reading and adapting to the enemy's intentions.
By relentlessly staying on the enemy's flank, you will eventually destroy their commander.
This is called achieving your objective through pure strategic cunning.
On the day you take command, seal the borders, destroy the official credentials, and cut off all unauthorized communication.
Be decisive in the war council so you control the situation.
If the enemy leaves an opening, rush through it.
Preempt the enemy by seizing what they value most, and time your moves to control when and where the battle happens.
Follow established principles while staying adaptive, and hold off until you can fight the decisive battle.
At first, be as elusive as a shy maiden — until the enemy drops their guard. Then strike with the speed of a sprinting hare, and it will be too late for the enemy to react.

chapters.title: XII — The Attack by Fire
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: There are five ways to attack with fire. First, burn the enemy's troops in camp. Second, burn their supplies. Third, burn their transport. Fourth, burn their arsenals and depots. Fifth, use fire projectiles against the enemy.
To execute a fire attack, you must have the right materials at hand.
Fire-starting equipment must always be kept ready.
There is a right season for fire attacks and specific days that favor them.
The right season is when the weather is very dry. The favorable days are when winds are rising — these can be calculated from astronomical patterns.
When attacking with fire, be prepared for five possible developments:
First: When fire breaks out inside the enemy camp, immediately launch your external attack.
Second: If fire erupts but the enemy's soldiers stay calm, hold back and wait. Do not attack prematurely.
Third: When the fire reaches peak intensity, follow up with an attack if practical. If not, hold your position.
Fourth: If you can start a fire from outside, do not wait for it to start from within. Attack when conditions are right.
A daytime wind lasts long; a night wind dies quickly.
In every campaign, the five developments of fire must be understood, the astronomical conditions monitored, and the right days anticipated.
Those who use fire as a weapon demonstrate intelligence. Those who use water as a weapon gain additional force.
Water can isolate an enemy, but it cannot destroy their resources.
It is a tragic waste to win battles and capture objectives but fail to follow through — this leads to stagnation and squandered opportunity.
The enlightened ruler plans far ahead. The effective commander develops his resources.
Do not move unless you see a clear advantage. Do not deploy troops unless there is something to gain. Do not fight unless the situation is critical.
No ruler should start a war out of anger. No commander should fight a battle out of spite.
Act when it serves your advantage. Stay put when it does not.
Anger fades. Irritation passes.
But a destroyed nation cannot be rebuilt. The dead cannot be brought back to life.
The wise ruler is therefore cautious, and the good commander is careful. This is how you protect the state and keep the army intact.

chapters.title: XIII — The Use of Spies
paragraphs: Sun Tzu said: Raising an army of a hundred thousand and marching them great distances imposes an enormous burden on the people and a massive drain on the state treasury. The cost runs to a thousand ounces of silver per day.
There will be disruption at home and abroad, and people will collapse from exhaustion along the roads.
As many as seven hundred thousand households will be disrupted from their work.

Armies may face each other for years, all for a victory decided in a single day. Given these stakes, to remain ignorant of the enemy's situation because you begrudge the cost of intelligence gathering is the height of irresponsibility.
A leader who operates this way is no real commander, no true asset to the sovereign, and no architect of victory.
What enables great leaders to strike with precision and achieve what ordinary people cannot is foreknowledge.
This foreknowledge cannot come from supernatural sources. It cannot be derived from analogy with past events. It cannot be calculated from theory.
Knowledge of the enemy's situation can only come from people.
Hence the use of spies, of which there are five types: (1) Local spies; (2) Inside spies; (3) Turned spies; (4) Expendable spies; (5) Surviving spies.
When all five types of spies are working simultaneously, the system becomes impenetrable. This is called the divine web of intelligence. It is a leader's most valuable asset.
Local spies are recruited from the local population.
Inside spies are recruited from the enemy's own officials.
Turned spies are enemy spies who have been captured and recruited to work for you.
Expendable spies are your own agents who are deliberately fed false information, allowed to leak it to the enemy — knowing they may be killed for it.
Surviving spies are those who successfully return with intelligence from the enemy camp.
No one in the entire army should be treated with closer attention than your spies.
No one should be more generously rewarded. No operation requires greater secrecy.
Spies cannot be effectively managed without keen intuition and judgment.
They cannot be properly handled without integrity and fair dealing.
Without sharp analytical thinking, you cannot determine the truth of their reports.
Be subtle! Be subtle! Use your intelligence network for every kind of operation.
If a spy reveals a secret before the time is right, both the spy and the person who received the information must be eliminated.

Whether your objective is to defeat an army, storm a city, or eliminate an individual, you must first identify the enemy commander's key staff — their aides, gatekeepers, and bodyguards. Your spies must be tasked with mapping these details.
Enemy spies operating against you must be found, bribed, and turned. Treat them well and settle them comfortably. This is how you create turned spies who now work for you.
Through turned spies, you gain the intelligence needed to recruit and deploy local and inside spies.
Through turned spies, you can feed false intelligence to expendable spies for them to deliver to the enemy.
Through turned spies, your surviving spies can be deployed at exactly the right moments.
The ultimate purpose of all five types of espionage is knowledge of the enemy. And that knowledge, in every case, traces back to the turned spy.
Therefore, the turned spy must be treated with the greatest generosity.
In ancient times, the rise of the Yin dynasty was made possible by Yi Zhi,
who had served under the Xia. Likewise, the rise of the Zhou dynasty was made possible by Lu Ya, who had served under the Yin.
Only the enlightened ruler and the brilliant commander will use the best minds in the army for intelligence work — and through it, achieve transformative results.
Spies are the most critical element in warfare, because the army's entire ability to act depends on the intelligence they provide.
